mainTopic: Why only a טמא נזיר is called a חוטא, and how each unclear phrase in the משנה (כזה, מסלסל, מכלכל, לשלח פרע, ציפורין) can mean accepting נזירות
overview: This amud starts by finishing an earlier question. Even רבי אלעזר הקפר, who calls a נזיר a חוטא, only means a נזיר who became טמא and must restart his count, since he might end up breaking his vow. A נזיר טהור is not called a sinner. Then the גמרא goes through the משנה's list of phrases that make someone a נזיר. For "הריני כזה," שמואל explains that a נזיר was walking past. For "מסלסל" and "מכלכל," the גמרא proves that each word can mean growing hair. Each word also has another meaning, honoring תורה or feeding the poor, so שמואל says the man was holding his hair. For "לשלח פרע," the גמרא proves that שלח means growth, first from a matching word פרע used for a נזיר and for a כהן, and then by rereading "שולח מים" as watering crops so they grow. Finally, ריש לקיש explains why רבי מאיר says "birds are upon me" makes a person a נזיר: a פסוק in דניאל places birds next to growing hair, and רבי מאיר holds that a person can link his vow to something placed next to it.

steps.title: Only an impure nazirite is called a sinner
steps.stepSummary: Even רבי אלעזר הקפר, who calls a נזיר a חוטא, only says this about a נזיר טמא, because restarting the count may lead him to break his vow. A נזיר טהור is not called a sinner.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. Even רבי אלעזר הקפר, who said a נזיר is a sinner, meant only an impure נזיר. Since he must cancel the days he already kept, as the תורה says, 'the first days will be void, because his נזירות was made impure,' he might come to break his נזירות. But a pure נזיר is not called a sinner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question raised just before this line. It explains that the 'sinner' label of רבי אלעזר הקפר only applies to a נזיר who became טמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נזיר who becomes טמא loses the days he already counted and must start over. His נזירות now lasts longer than he planned, so he may give up and break it. That risk is why he is called a חוטא. A נזיר טהור has no such risk, so the label does not apply to him.

keyTerms.meaning: A נזיר who became ritually impure (for example, from a dead body)
To cancel (here, the days of נזירות already kept)
'The Merciful One,' meaning the תורה, or ה׳ speaking in it
To break his vow of נזירות

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי אלעזר הקפר, the 'sinner' label belongs only to a נזיר טמא, because restarting his count might lead him to break his vow. A נזיר טהור is not called a חוטא.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי אלעזר הקפר says every נזיר is a sinner. Here the גמרא limits his statement to a נזיר who became טמא.

phrases.english: Yes, for even according to רבי אלעזר הקפר
who said: a nazirite is a sinner,
that applies only to an impure nazirite,
since he needs to cancel his days,
phrases.notes: He has to throw away the days he already counted and start his נזירות over.

phrases.english: as the Merciful One says:
"But the first days will be void, because his consecration was defiled",

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם הוּא, דִּלְמָא אָתֵי לְמִיעְבַּר עַל נְזִירוּתֵיהּ,
phrases.english: it is there that perhaps he will come to break his nazirite vow,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל נָזִיר טָהוֹר — לָאו חוֹטֵא קָרֵי בֵּיהּ.
phrases.english: but a pure nazirite — he does not call him a sinner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised just before this section of the daf.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. The 'sinner' label applies only to a נזיר טמא, who may break his longer vow. A נזיר טהור is not called a חוטא.

steps.title: How can 'I am like this' mean nazirite?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה's phrase "הריני כזה." Even if the man is holding his hair, his words never clearly say he means a נזיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said "I am like this" makes a person a נזיר. Granted, he is holding his hair. But he only said 'I am like this.' He did not say that he means a נזיר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns back to the משנה's list of phrases and questions "הריני כזה." It doubts that these vague words can create נזירות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Grabbing his hair might hint at hair, but the words 'like this' never mention נזירות. So the גמרא asks how such an unclear statement can count as a vow.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I am hereby like this,' one of the משנה's phrases
'Granted, even if...,' which concedes a point before challenging

phrases.english: "I am hereby like this" —
granted that he is holding his hair,
"I am hereby like this" — he did not say!
phrases.notes: The point: holding his hair does not make 'like this' clearly mean a נזיר.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new phrase from the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that "הריני כזה" makes a person a נזיר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The words are too vague. Holding his hair does not show he meant נזירות.

steps.title: A nazirite was passing by
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains that a נזיר was walking past when the man spoke, so 'like this' clearly means 'like him.'
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: This is a case where a נזיר was passing in front of him.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the challenge by describing the exact situation in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words alone are vague, but the setting makes them clear. When a נזיר is right there, 'I am like this' can only mean 'I am a נזיר like him.'

keyTerms.meaning: 'For example,' which introduces the specific case

steps.whatToRemember: "הריני כזה" counts as a נזירות vow when a נזיר is passing by, because the setting shows what he means.

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
For example, where a nazirite was passing before him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: כְּגוֹן שֶׁהָיָה נָזִיר עוֹבֵר לְפָנָיו
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Like this' is too vague to count as a נזירות vow.
steps.terutzMaskana: With a נזיר passing by, 'like this' clearly means 'like this נזיר.'

steps.title: Does 'curler' really refer to hair?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that "מסלסל" in the משנה means growing or curling hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said "I am a curler" makes a person a נזיר. How do we know this word means curling hair?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next phrase in the משנה and asks for proof of what the word means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word "מסלסל" could have more than one meaning. The גמרא wants a source showing that people used it to mean growing out hair.

keyTerms.meaning: Curling, which here means growing out one's hair

phrases.english: "I am hereby a curler" —
from where do we know that this means curling of hair?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next phrase in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Proof that "מסלסל" means growing or curling hair.

steps.title: Proof from the maidservant of רבי
steps.stepSummary: The maidservant in רבי's house used the word this way: "Until when will you curl your hair?" So "מסלסל" is everyday language for growing hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the maidservant of רבי's house said to a certain man: Until when will you curl your hair?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by showing how real people spoke. The word was used for letting hair grow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vows follow the way people actually talk. The maidservant in רבי's house used "מסלסל" for hair, which shows the word carries this meaning in everyday speech.

keyTerms.meaning: The maidservant of רבי יהודה הנשיא's household

phrases.aramaic: כְּדַאֲמַרָה לֵיהּ הָהִיא אַמְּתָא דְבֵי רַבִּי
phrases.english: As that maidservant of the house of Rabbi said
to a certain man:
Until when will you curl your hair?

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדַאֲמַרָה לֵיהּ הָהִיא אַמְּתָא דְבֵי רַבִּי
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Everyday speech, shown by the maidservant's words, uses "מסלסל" for growing hair.

steps.title: Maybe 'curler' means honoring Torah
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: "מסלסל" might mean honoring תורה, as in the פסוק "סלסלה ותרוממך."
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead that it means תורה, as it is written: "Extol her and she will exalt you."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises another possible meaning of the word, which would weaken the proof from the maidservant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if "מסלסל" can mean growing hair, it also appears in a פסוק about honoring תורה. So a man who says "I am a מסלסל" might mean he will honor תורה, not that he is taking on נזירות.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Say instead,' which suggests a different reading
'Extol her and she will exalt you,' a פסוק about תורה

phrases.english: Say that it means Torah,
as it is written: "Extol her and she will exalt you"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the meaning proven in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that "מסלסל" in the משנה means growing hair
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word also means honoring תורה, so it is unclear which meaning the speaker intended.

steps.title: He was holding his hair
steps.stepSummary: שמואל answers that here too the man was holding his hair, which shows he meant hair and not תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: Here too, it is a case where he was holding his hair.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל settles the question by again pointing to the setting: the man held his hair as he spoke.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding his hair rules out the תורה meaning. So "מסלסל" clearly means letting his hair grow, which is נזירות.
steps.whatToRemember: Unclear phrases count as נזירות vows when the setting makes the meaning clear: a נזיר passing by, or the speaker holding his hair.

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
Here too, where he is holding his hair.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הָכָא נָמֵי שֶׁתָּפוּס בִּשְׂעָרוֹ
steps.terutzMaskana: He was holding his hair, so he clearly meant growing hair, which is נזירות.

steps.title: How do we know 'מכלכל' means growing hair?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source showing that the word 'מכלכל' in the משנה refers to growing hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said that someone who says 'I am hereby מכלכל' becomes a נזיר. How do we know this word is about growing his hair?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next phrase in the משנה, 'הריני מכלכל,' and asks how we know it means growing hair. This sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same pattern we saw with 'מסלסל.' A person only becomes a נזיר if his words clearly point to נזירות, so the גמרא needs to show that 'מכלכל' is really a hair word.

keyTerms.meaning: Growing or tending hair (the word being explained)
The noun form: growth or care of hair

phrases.english: "I am hereby growing [my hair]"
From where do we know that this is a term for growing his hair?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing 'מסלסל,' the גמרא applies the same question to the next phrase in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that כילכול refers to hair.

steps.title: Proof from the משנה about carrying lime on שבת
steps.stepSummary: A משנה in שבת measures lime by 'enough to smear on a כילכול,' and רב explains that this is the hair area near the temples.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in a משנה about lime: רבי יהודה says the amount is enough to smear on a כילכול. And רב said this means the area under the temple.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by quoting a משנה where the word כילכול shows up, together with רב's explanation that it refers to hair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה uses כילכול as a normal word, and רב explains that it means the hair beneath the temple. Since the word is used for a spot of hair, 'מכלכל' in our משנה can mean growing hair.

keyTerms.meaning: The area beneath the temple, where hair grows

phrases.english: As we learned in a משנה:
Lime: רבי יהודה says:
phrases.notes: This משנה is in שבת 78b, about how much lime you have to carry out on שבת to be liable.

phrases.english: Enough to smear on a kilkul.
And רב said: the area beneath the temple.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדִתְנַן: סִיד, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: כְּדֵי לָסוּד כִּילְכּוּל
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word כילכול is used in a משנה, and רב explains it as the hair beneath the temple.

steps.title: Maybe 'מכלכל' means feeding the poor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that 'כלכל' can also mean supporting people, as when יוסף supported his family.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say that he meant he would feed poor people, as the פסוק says: 'And יוסף sustained his father and his brothers.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the proof by showing that the same root also means feeding and supporting people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 showed that the word can mean hair, but this פסוק shows that it can also mean support. If the word has two meanings, then saying 'מכלכל' might not clearly mean נזירות.

keyTerms.meaning: And he sustained or provided for

phrases.english: Say [he meant] feeding the poor,
as it is written:
"And יוסף sustained his father and his brothers."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof of step 9 with a second possible meaning.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'מכלכל' clearly refers to hair.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The root כלכל also means to sustain people, so the vow could be about charity and not hair.

steps.title: שמואל: he was holding his hair
steps.stepSummary: שמואל answers that the man was holding his hair when he spoke, so he clearly meant hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: here too, he was holding his hair.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל resolves the challenge with the same answer he gave for 'מסלסל': the man's actions show what he meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל does not deny that the word could mean feeding. He explains that the משנה is a case where the man was holding his hair, which removes any doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: That he was holding his hair

steps.whatToRemember: For both 'מסלסל' and 'מכלכל,' the word alone could have another meaning. The man's action of holding his hair is what makes it clear he means נזירות.

phrases.english: שמואל said:
Here too, it is where he was holding his hair.
phrases.notes: 'Here too' points back to step 7, where שמואל gave this same answer for 'מסלסל.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הָכָא נָמֵי שֶׁתָּפוּס בִּשְׂעָרוֹ
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the man's action makes his meaning clear.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'מכלכל' might mean feeding the poor.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because he was holding his hair, he clearly meant growing hair.

steps.title: How do we know 'לשלח' means growing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next phrase in the משנה, 'הרי עלי לשלח פרע,' and asks how we know 'שלוח' means growth.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'It is upon me to grow long hair,' and he is a נזיר. How do we know that this word שלוח means growth?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next phrase in the משנה and asks for a source that 'שלוח' means increasing. This sets up the proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'לשלח' usually suggests sending. To treat it as a נזירות vow, the גמרא needs to show that it can also mean making something grow.

phrases.english: "It is upon me to grow long hair"
He is a נזיר.
From where do we know that this shiluach means growth?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new phrase from the משנה, examined in the same way as the earlier ones.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that שלוח means growth.

steps.title: Proof from שיר השירים: 'Your shoots are an orchard'
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'שלחיך פרדס רמונים' uses the root שלח for growing plants.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by quoting a פסוק where the root שלח describes growth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this פסוק, 'שלחיך' means things that grow out and spread. That shows the root can mean increase, so 'לשלח פרע' can mean letting hair grow long.

phrases.english: As it is written:
"Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates."

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק uses שלח to describe growing plants, so it can mean growth.

steps.title: Maybe 'לשלח' means sending something away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the proof: the root שלח can mean moving something away, as in sending water over the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say it means something about sending away, as the פסוק says: 'And He sends water over the fields.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof in step 13 by showing another meaning of the same root. Steps 15 and 16 answer this challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this פסוק, 'שולח' means moving water from one place to another. If that is the meaning, 'לשלח פרע' could mean sending the hair away, which is cutting it off, the opposite of נזירות.
steps.confusionAlert: This challenge does not stand. The גמרא gives two answers right after it: the matching word פרע (step 15), and a rereading of 'שולח מים' as growth (step 16).

phrases.english: Say it means something about removing,
as it is written:
"And He sends water over the fields"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof of step 13 with another meaning of the root.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'לשלח פרע' clearly means growing hair.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שלח can mean moving something away, so the vow might mean removing hair and not growing it.

steps.title: The word פרע links a נזיר to a כהן
steps.stepSummary: The תנא learns the meaning from a גזירה שוה. The word פרע by a נזיר means growing hair, so the same word by a כהן also means growing hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תנא learns it from 'פרע' and 'פרע.' Here, by a נזיר, it says 'He shall be holy, he shall let his locks grow.' There, by an ordinary כהן, it says 'and they shall not let their locks grow long.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 14. It no longer relies on the root שלח alone. Instead, it uses a matching word, פרע, to prove that the phrase is about growing hair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge in step 14 was that שלח could mean 'sending away.' The answer brings in the word פרע, which appears both by a נזיר and by a כהן. By a נזיר, פרע clearly means growing long hair, so 'פרע לא ישלחו' by the כהן must also mean letting hair grow. That shows 'לשלח פרע' is about growing hair.

keyTerms.meaning: The teacher of the משנה or ברייתא
An ordinary כהן, not the כהן גדול
'It is written here… and it is written there.' This is the formula for a word-match proof.

steps.whyThisMatters: It secures the משנה's ruling that 'הרי עלי לשלח פרע' is a valid way of accepting נזירות.

phrases.english: The tanna derives it from "pera" and "pera."
phrases.notes: He learns the meaning by matching the same word in two different פסוקים.

phrases.english: It is written here,
"He shall be holy, he shall let his locks grow long,"
and it is written there regarding an ordinary priest:
"and they shall not let their locks grow long."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 14 against the proof from 'שלחיך'
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replaces the weak proof with a stronger word-match (גזירה שוה)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שלח might mean sending away, so 'לשלח פרע' might not mean growing hair
steps.terutzMaskana: The word פרע by a נזיר and by a כהן shows that 'שילוח פרע' means growing hair

steps.title: Even 'שולח מים' means growth
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the פסוק about sending water is itself about growth, because watering makes produce grow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you want, say that 'sends water' also means growth. As רב יוסף translated it: when you water the produce, it grows.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different answer to the challenge from step 14. It says the very פסוק used in the challenge actually supports the meaning 'growth.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge used 'שולח מים' to argue that שלח means sending something away. This answer turns that around. רב יוסף's Aramaic translation shows the פסוק is talking about watering crops so they grow. So the root שלח still points to growth.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you want, say.' This introduces a second answer.

steps.whatToRemember: There are two answers to the challenge from step 14. One is the matching word פרע. The other shows that 'שולח מים' itself means watering for growth.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
this "sends water" is also a term of growth,
phrases.notes: This is the same פסוק the challenge used in step 14.

phrases.english: (as Rav Yosef translated:)
phrases.notes: These words in round brackets are in the printed גמרא, but some versions leave them out.

phrases.aramaic: דְּכַד מַשְׁקִין לֵיהּ מַיָּא לְפֵירָא וְרָבֵי.
phrases.english: that when one waters the produce, it grows.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא הַאי ״שׁוֹלֵחַ מַיִם״ נָמֵי רִיבּוּי הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the same challenge that step 15 answered
steps.terutzMaskana: 'שולח מים' means watering so that crops grow, so שלח means growth
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the reading of 'שולח מים' given in step 14

steps.title: Why does רבי מאיר say 'birds' makes a נזיר?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next case in the משנה, 'הרי עלי ציפורין,' where רבי מאיר says the person is a נזיר. It asks for his reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Birds are upon me.' רבי מאיר says: he is a נזיר. What is רבי מאיר's reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to a new case in the משנה. It asks why mentioning birds would make someone a נזיר. This step sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Birds seem to have nothing to do with נזירות. If anything, they sound like a קרבן. So the גמרא needs to explain how רבי מאיר links birds to growing hair.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is upon me.' This is the language of taking on a vow.

phrases.english: "Birds are upon me":
Rabbi Meir says: he is a nazirite.
What is the reason of Rabbi Meir?

steps.title: Birds sit next to hair in a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש explains that the person meant the birds that a פסוק places right next to growing hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: he took upon himself the birds that are placed next to hair. As it is written, 'until his hair grew like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws.'
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש answers the question. He shows a פסוק that puts growing hair and birds side by side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק in דניאל, the hair growing long and the 'birds' appear in the same verse. So when the person says 'birds,' he is pointing to that pair, and his real meaning is growing hair. That is נזירות.

steps.title: The principle behind רבי מאיר's view
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר holds that a person can link his vow to something that sits next to it in a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר holds: a person attaches his vow to something that is next to it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sums up the general rule behind רבי מאיר's ruling. This also explains why the חכמים disagree with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש's answer depends on a bigger idea. A person's words can refer to something that only sits next to them in a פסוק. רבי מאיר accepts that idea. The חכמים, who say he is not a נזיר, do not.
